title: Aurora Health x Redwood — RAG+Agent quickstart template technical deep dive
summary: Aurora Health requested a technical walkthrough of Redwood’s combined RAG+agents quickstart template with emphasis on (1) how retrieval is exposed as a tool in an agent workflow, (2) what telemetry is emitted out-of-the-box (OpenTelemetry traces/metrics/log fields) and how it maps to Redwood Console, and (3) constraints for Private deployment (VPC connectivity, secrets/KMS, audit logging, data retention/PII). Redwood covered the default template architecture (API service + ingestion worker + vector store adapter), safe defaults (timeouts, retries/backoff, tool allow-list, prompt injection guardrails), and how to run in Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Aurora asked about HIPAA considerations, whether prompts/responses are stored, and how to ensure correlation IDs and trace context propagate through a reverse proxy. Next steps focused on sharing the template repo links + observability pack, confirming Private network requirements, and scheduling a short validation run using Aurora’s staging docs set.
topics: Combined RAG+agent template architecture (retrieval tool, planner/executor, ingestion)
Observability: OTel tracing, metrics, structured logs, correlation IDs, token/cost attribution
Private deployment constraints: VPC/on-prem options, KMS/HSM, audit logs, data retention
Safety defaults: tool allow-list, tool timeouts, schema validation, prompt injection guidance
Vector store backend defaults and extension points
Operational guardrails: rate-limit handling (429), retries/backoff, streaming disconnect behavior
next_steps: Redwood to email Aurora links to the combined RAG+agent quickstart template, observability pack import instructions, and the telemetry contract v1 reference.
Aurora to confirm target Private deployment shape (single VPC vs multi-VPC, egress rules, whether on-prem is required) and preferred secrets/KMS approach.
Aurora to provide a small non-PHI document set for initial ingestion/perf test and a target latency/cost envelope for the support-agent workflow.
Schedule a 30-minute follow-up to review the first run results and align on Dedicated vs Private path (and any HIPAA BA/security addenda items).
action_items: Avery Johnson - Send follow-up email with template links, Console screenshots of dashboards, and basic sizing notes - due 2026-01-19
Logan Wright - Share trace/metric field list (telemetry contract v1) and cardinality guidance for tenant/request/model tags - due 2026-01-19
Kira Thompson - Outline Private deployment prerequisites (networking, KMS, audit logs, retention) for Aurora’s security review packet - due 2026-01-22
Priya Nair - Confirm Aurora’s preferred vector DB option (managed vs self-hosted) and whether pgvector is acceptable for first pilot - due 2026-01-23
transcript:
Meeting: Aurora Health x Redwood — RAG+Agent quickstart template technical deep dive
Recorded: 2026-01-18 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 min
Attendees:
- Redwood: Avery Johnson (AE), Renee Sullivan (Dev Advocate / SE), Kira Thompson (Private deployments), Logan Wright (Telemetry)
- Aurora Health: Priya Nair (Data Platform), Jenna Liu (ML Eng), Michael Reyes (Security), Tom Alvarez (DevOps)

Auto Summary (Fireflies):
- Aurora wants to validate Redwood quickstart templates for a "support agent" style workflow (ticket + internal docs).
- Key questions: observability and Private deployment constraints for regulated environment.

Questions captured:
- Does the combined template store prompts/responses anywhere by default?
- How do you keep trace context and request_id consistent through a proxy / gateway?
- Can the retrieval step be forced to use only approved corp sources?
- What changes between Hosted API usage vs Private runtime?

Transcript:

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, cool. I think we’re good to start. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is a technical deep dive on the combined RAG plus agent quickstart template—what it actually does, what you get for telemetry, and then Kira can cover Private constraints, right.

[00:13] Priya Nair: Yep. Thanks Avery. We’ve looked at a bunch of like LangChain examples and, honestly, they’re… they’re kind of toy-ish. We want something that looks like what we’d deploy.

[00:24] Renee Sullivan: Totally. That’s exactly why we made these. They’re opinionated. We’re trying not to teach bad patterns.

[00:31] Jenna Liu: Can you start with the architecture of the combined one? Like what processes are running.

[00:36] Renee Sullivan: Yeah. So the combined template is basically three pieces. One is an API service—FastAPI in Python in the Python version, or a Node service in TypeScript. Second is an ingestion worker that takes documents, chunks them, creates embeddings, writes to a vector store. Third is a vector store adapter layer.

[00:55] Renee Sullivan: Then for the “agent” part, the retrieval is exposed as a tool. So the model can call something like `retrieval.search(query, filters)` and we wrap that tool with timeouts, allow-listing, and output schema validation.

[01:09] Tom Alvarez: When you say “tool”, that’s like function calling, right?

[01:12] Renee Sullivan: Exactly. Redwood Hosted API supports tool calling / structured outputs. The template uses that. And importantly, we do NOT allow arbitrary tools by default. It’s like a small allow-list: retrieve, maybe “get_ticket” in the reference app, and that’s it.

[01:28] Michael Reyes: Before we go too far: where does the data go? Like prompts, responses, document content, any of it stored in Redwood? By default?

[01:38] Avery Johnson: Good call. For Hosted API, request/response is processed by Redwood; we have retention controls and enterprise options, but let’s separate product policy from template behavior.

[01:48] Kira Thompson: On template behavior: the template itself doesn’t persist prompts/responses unless you turn on debug logging or you add your own storage. It emits structured logs and traces; we recommend redacting PII and not logging full prompts. The README calls that out.

[02:04] Logan Wright: And on telemetry, we emit metadata like model name, route, token usage counters, latency buckets—stuff like that. Not the full text by default.

[02:15] Michael Reyes: Okay. So you’re not logging body content to some third party collector by default.

[02:19] Logan Wright: Correct—unless you configure it to. In our sample OTel config, we ship traces/metrics to a local collector in Docker Compose, and you can swap that to your internal collector.

[02:30] Priya Nair: We’re interested in Private, but we might start with Hosted for a pilot. What changes when we go Private? Like do we lose features.

[02:39] Kira Thompson: The quick answer: same API contract and same telemetry contract. Differences are operational: you run the control plane in your environment, you manage networking, and you decide where telemetry goes. You can still use the Console, depending on the Private setup—some customers keep it fully internal; some allow outbound to Redwood Console endpoints.

[02:58] Tom Alvarez: We’d probably want no outbound from the inference cluster. Like… strict.

[03:03] Kira Thompson: Yep. Then you’d keep telemetry internal. The templates are built with OpenTelemetry specifically so you can point it at your SIEM / observability stack.

[03:13] Jenna Liu: On the agent flow—can you describe it? Like does it do planning or is it just “call retrieve then answer.”

[03:20] Renee Sullivan: The default is intentionally simple. It’s a planner/executor-ish pattern but lightweight. The system prompt tells it: first decide whether you need retrieval; if yes, call retrieval tool; then ground the answer using cited chunks; if the tool fails, degrade gracefully and tell the user.

[03:39] Renee Sullivan: We also add prompt injection guidance: treat retrieved text as untrusted, don’t follow instructions inside documents, don’t exfiltrate secrets. We can’t prevent everything, but we give the pattern.

[03:55] Priya Nair: What about restricting retrieval to “approved corp sources”? We have multiple repositories and PHI boundaries.

[04:03] Renee Sullivan: The tool signature supports filters. Like `tenant_id`, `corpus`, `doc_acl` tags. The adapter passes that to the vector store query. The template includes a place where you attach auth context from your gateway and map that into retrieval filters.

[04:21] Logan Wright: And those tags show up as attributes on spans/metrics too, but we strongly recommend low-cardinality. Like `tenant_id` is ok if it’s a handful; not ok if it’s millions.

[04:32] Jenna Liu: So you’re saying we should not put patient_id there.

[04:35] Logan Wright: Exactly. No patient IDs in trace tags.

[04:39] Michael Reyes: +1, please no.

[04:41] Avery Johnson: Yep.

[04:45] Tom Alvarez: What vector DB is the default? We don’t want to adopt something exotic just for a template.

[04:51] Renee Sullivan: For v1 we picked a common backend. In the Python template we support Postgres + pgvector as a default path and then an adapter interface where you can plug in something else. Some folks use Pinecone or Weaviate; we didn’t want 12 options out of the gate.

[05:09] Tom Alvarez: pgvector is fine for us if it’s self-hosted.

[05:12] Priya Nair: We have Postgres already. Okay.

[05:15] Jenna Liu: How do you handle ingestion? Like chunk sizes, embeddings, etc.

[05:20] Renee Sullivan: The ingestion worker has sane defaults: chunk size, overlap, normalization. It uses the embeddings endpoint and writes vectors + metadata. Also has backpressure, and it’s idempotent-ish—like it won’t keep duplicating if you re-run with same doc IDs.

[05:39] Jenna Liu: And evals? We need some regression test because clinicians will complain if it hallucinates.

[05:45] Renee Sullivan: There’s hooks for an eval harness config. It’s minimal: a prompt set and expected citations. Not a full eval framework. But it’s enough to catch “retrieval broke” or “agent started calling tool 10 times.”

[06:03] Priya Nair: Observability is a big thing for us. Specifically, can we attribute cost per route, per tenant, and we need to debug latency spikes.

[06:12] Logan Wright: That’s what the telemetry contract is about. The template emits metrics like request latency (p50/p95), token counts input/output, and error counts broken down by error_class. For traces, every request has a root span with attributes like `request_id`, `tenant`, `model`, `route`, `deployment_mode`.

[06:33] Logan Wright: There’s also child spans around: vector search, rerank (if enabled), LLM call, streaming write. So you can see where time goes.

[06:44] Tom Alvarez: Do you propagate `traceparent`?

[06:46] Logan Wright: Yes. In the templates we read inbound `traceparent` and we also generate one if missing. We also echo back a `x-request-id` and we include it in logs.

[06:58] Michael Reyes: We terminate TLS at our gateway. Sometimes headers get stripped. Is there a required header list?

[07:05] Logan Wright: For best results: `traceparent`, `tracestate` if you have it, and `x-request-id`. Also if you have a tenant header, pass it through. The docs say exactly what to forward.

[07:17] Avery Johnson: We’ve seen that be a common gotcha—proxies dropping trace headers.

[07:23] Priya Nair: Is there a Redwood-specific correlation ID we have to use? Or can we use our own.

[07:28] Logan Wright: You can use your own. The template will respect an inbound `x-request-id`. We also generate one if absent, but we don’t force you to use ours.

[07:38] Jenna Liu: Can you talk about error taxonomy? Like we don’t want “500” for everything.

[07:44] Renee Sullivan: Totally. The templates wrap errors into a few classes: rate_limit (429), timeout, upstream_unavailable, validation_error, tool_error, and unknown. We also include a stable error code string so support tickets are easier.

[08:02] Tom Alvarez: And retries? Particularly 429.

[08:05] Renee Sullivan: Default policy is exponential backoff with jitter, respect `Retry-After` if provided, max attempts is low to avoid thundering herd. We also recommend a client-side circuit breaker if you’re saturating.

[08:21] Priya Nair: What about streaming? We’ve had streaming disconnects with some providers when behind corporate proxies.

[08:28] Renee Sullivan: Yeah, it happens. The SDK helper includes a “reconnect on retryable disconnect” pattern for streaming, but it’s careful: it won’t double-execute tools. That’s where idempotency matters.

[08:42] Jenna Liu: Wait, how do you prevent double tool calls if you reconnect?

[08:46] Renee Sullivan: The template uses idempotency keys and keeps tool calls deterministic-ish by doing tool execution server-side once per request_id. If the client reconnects, it resumes the stream from the server buffer. If you can’t buffer, then you disable that and accept that streaming is best-effort.

[09:09] Tom Alvarez: Okay so there is buffering.

[09:11] Renee Sullivan: Optional. Default for dev is small buffer.

[09:15] Michael Reyes: On Private, do we have to run your Console? Or can we use Splunk / Datadog and call it a day.

[09:22] Kira Thompson: You can do either. Private deployment doesn’t require Console. But Console is useful for model routing/fallback policies and for the “token cost breakdown” view—depending on how you integrate. Some Private customers export the same metrics to both places.

[09:39] Priya Nair: We’re HIPAA covered. So we need to understand if prompts can contain PHI. In theory yes. In practice we’ll try not to.

[09:47] Kira Thompson: Understood. For Private, you control the environment so PHI stays in your network. For Hosted, we’d need to align on the right commercial and security terms, and we’d strongly recommend PHI redaction before sending requests unless you have an agreement in place.

[10:07] Michael Reyes: Also retention: do you store prompts.

[10:10] Avery Johnson: For Hosted, we have configurable retention and enterprise controls; for this call, we can follow up with the security packet. The templates themselves are built so you don’t log content.

[10:22] Priya Nair: Ok. Can we talk about “Private constraints.” Like network, KMS, audit logs.

[10:28] Kira Thompson: Sure. For Private in a VPC, typical requirements: outbound network can be fully blocked, but you’ll need access to model weights storage (either your own object store or a mirrored registry) and whatever vector DB you use. Secrets: we integrate with KMS/HSM depending on your stack. Audit logs: we recommend shipping access logs and admin actions into your SIEM, and the templates include guidance to put request_id and tenant in logs.

[10:56] Tom Alvarez: What about Kubernetes. Are the manifests in the template production ready.

[11:01] Kira Thompson: They’re minimal. They include readiness/liveness, resource requests, and a deployment + service. Not a full Helm chart. For production you’d wrap it with your policies.

[11:15] Tom Alvarez: Any GPU requirements for the app pieces.

[11:18] Renee Sullivan: The app doesn’t need GPU. It calls Redwood for inference. In Private, your inference cluster has GPUs; the app can run on CPU.

[11:28] Jenna Liu: For latency, where do you usually see bottlenecks. Retrieval, inference, network.

[11:34] Renee Sullivan: Honestly, all three. Retrieval is sometimes the surprise if you have a slow vector DB. Also chunking too large increases context tokens which increases inference cost and latency.

[11:48] Logan Wright: That’s why the default dashboards have separate panels: retrieval latency, model latency, token counts, and error rate. It’s easier to see what changed.

[12:00] Priya Nair: Do you provide those dashboards.

[12:02] Logan Wright: Yep, there’s an “observability pack” JSON you can import. It assumes the telemetry contract field names. It’s meant to work out of the box.

[12:13] Michael Reyes: Is there PII risk in traces? Like if someone accidentally puts doc text in span attributes.

[12:20] Logan Wright: We try hard to keep it out. The templates do not attach prompt text to spans. We also include a note: don’t put raw user input in attributes, use hash or length metrics. But it’s ultimately developer-controlled.

[12:37] Priya Nair: In your combined flow, do you do reranking.

[12:41] Renee Sullivan: Optional. Default is top-k vector search. There’s a toggle to add reranking, but it’s off by default to keep cost predictable.

[12:54] Jenna Liu: And citations.

[12:56] Renee Sullivan: Yes, it returns answer plus citations (doc id + chunk offsets). In the agent prompt we instruct it to cite.

[13:07] Tom Alvarez: Can we customize the tool schema. Like add a “create ticket” tool later.

[13:11] Renee Sullivan: Yep. But we recommend: start with retrieval only. Then add tools one at a time, always with allow-list, timeouts, and schema validation.

[13:25] Michael Reyes: Are there defaults for tool timeouts.

[13:27] Renee Sullivan: Yep—tools have a hard timeout wrapper. I think it’s 3 seconds by default for retrieval in dev; you can bump. We also bound retries so you don’t get tool loops.

[13:42] Jenna Liu: Tool loops is exactly what we’re worried about.

[13:45] Renee Sullivan: We also cap max tool calls per request. And the eval hook includes a test that the agent doesn’t call retrieve more than N times.

[14:00] Priya Nair: That’s good.

[14:02] Avery Johnson: Do you want to go deeper on Private? Or should we do a small “walkthrough” of telemetry fields.

[14:08] Priya Nair: Telemetry fields. Specifically, can we track tenant, route, model, and token usage. And we need a correlation ID we can pass from our UI to the backend to inference.

[14:19] Logan Wright: Yep. The core ones:
- `request_id` (string)
- `tenant` (string)
- `route` (string)
- `model` (string)
- `region` (string)
- `deployment_mode` (hosted/dedicated/private)
- token usage: input_tokens, output_tokens, total_tokens
- latency_ms for end-to-end and per stage

[14:45] Logan Wright: Logs also include `error_class` and `error_code`. Metrics include counters for 429s and timeouts.

[14:55] Tom Alvarez: Cardinality again. So if tenant is like… we have 40 hospitals, that’s okay.

[15:01] Logan Wright: 40 is fine. 40k is not.

[15:05] Jenna Liu: For cost attribution—does Redwood Console give you per request cost.

[15:10] Avery Johnson: Yes for Hosted and Dedicated. For Private, depending on configuration, you can still get token-level cost breakdowns, but it’s a bit more of an integration conversation.

[15:22] Priya Nair: We’d likely want it internal anyway.

[15:26] Logan Wright: Even if internal, tokens are emitted as metrics so you can build cost dashboards. You’d multiply by your pricing model or compute GPU amortized cost.

[15:40] Michael Reyes: Switching back: audit logs. For Private, can we get admin action logs. Like model changes.

[15:46] Kira Thompson: Yes. Private control plane logs can be shipped to your SIEM. Also we recommend RBAC and SSO/SAML in enterprise setups. We can cover specifics offline.

[16:03] Priya Nair: Another question: We might need multi-region for disaster recovery. Does template handle that.

[16:10] Renee Sullivan: The template itself is stateless, so you can deploy in two regions. For inference, Redwood has routing/fallback policies. In Private, you can set up routing across clusters, but that’s more involved.

[16:26] Tom Alvarez: Is that like global load balancer.

[16:28] Kira Thompson: Exactly. Plus model version pinning so behavior stays consistent.

[16:36] Jenna Liu: Do you pin model version in the template.

[16:39] Renee Sullivan: Yes. The config includes model name and optionally a version tag. We recommend pinning so your evals stay stable.

[16:52] Priya Nair: Great.

[16:54] Michael Reyes: On security: secrets management. The templates use .env files?

[16:59] Renee Sullivan: For local dev, yes. But we include a policy: .env is in .gitignore, and there’s notes about using a secret manager in real deploys. CI includes secret scanning config.

[17:16] Tom Alvarez: That’s good.

[17:18] Jenna Liu: Do you do any PII redaction automatically.

[17:22] Renee Sullivan: We include guidance and a hook. We don’t ship a full redaction model in the template.

[17:31] Priya Nair: Okay.

[17:33] Avery Johnson: We’ve covered a lot. Are there any hard blockers you want to flag now.

[17:39] Michael Reyes: For us, it’s basically: if we can’t do Private with no outbound network, it’s a problem.

[17:46] Kira Thompson: Understood. That’s supported. We’ll outline prerequisites and what you would host.

[17:54] Tom Alvarez: Also we want to be clear that the template is not calling random internet tools.

[17:59] Renee Sullivan: Yeah, no. Default is only retrieval tool and it’s against your own vector DB.

[18:05] Jenna Liu: Can you send a link to the repo and a diagram. Our architects will ask.

[18:10] Avery Johnson: Yep. We’ll send the links and the short architecture diagram from the docs.

[18:16] Priya Nair: And if we start with Hosted for a pilot, can we keep the same code when moving to Private.

[18:22] Renee Sullivan: Yes, that’s a design goal. Same env var contract, same request headers, same telemetry schema. You basically change endpoints and auth.

[18:34] Logan Wright: Telemetry stays. Just point the exporter to a different collector.

[18:39] Priya Nair: Okay.

[18:41] (cross talk)

[18:44] Tom Alvarez: One more: does the template have health checks and graceful shutdown.

[18:49] Renee Sullivan: Yes. There’s `/healthz` and `/readyz`. Shutdown drains in-flight requests and flushes telemetry.

[18:58] Tom Alvarez: Perfect.

[19:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, I’m going to jump to next steps and then we can use remaining time for any deep questions. Next steps: we’ll send the quickstart links, the observability pack, and Kira will follow with a Private constraints checklist.

[19:16] Priya Nair: Sounds good.

[19:18] Jenna Liu: Actually can we quickly talk about “prompt injection” again. Like is there anything besides a warning.

[19:24] Renee Sullivan: It’s partly a warning, partly a pattern. We separate “instructions” from “data” in the prompt, we explicitly tell the model to ignore instructions in retrieved docs, and we validate tool outputs against JSON schema. That reduces some classes of attacks. But if you want stronger defenses, you add content filtering and maybe retrieval-time sanitization.

[19:52] Michael Reyes: Okay.

[19:54] Priya Nair: That’s fine for v1.

[20:00] Avery Johnson: Cool. Any other questions.

[20:04] (brief silence)

[20:07] Tom Alvarez: Not now.

[20:09] Priya Nair: We’ll review what you send and come back.

[20:13] Avery Johnson: Great. Thanks everyone.

[20:16] Fireflies note: Transcript continues with small talk / scheduling details; omitted for brevity.

(End of transcript export)
